newsitem.title: FRANCE: Accord near on resumption of Paris-Algiers flights.
newsitem.headline: Accord near on resumption of Paris-Algiers flights.

text.p: France and Algeria are near agreement on a resumption of flights by Algeria's national airline between Paris and Algiers, halted in 1995 in a dispute over security, French officials said on Tuesday.
They said talks were on course for Air Algerie to provide three or four round-trip flights a day to the French capital beginning around April 1.
But Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt denied a published report that an agreement had been concluded.
"The project is heading in the right direction," said one official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"As recently as two weeks ago, it appeared the Algerians were dragging their feet. But now all parties are working together to make a resumption of service possible as of April 1," the official said.
Air Algerie had no immediate comment.

Transport officials said the French Foreign Ministry seemed particularly eager to show progress in the talks, which have dragged on for more than a year during a time of frayed ties between Paris and its former North African colony.
France ended all flights by French airlines to Algeria following the December 1994 hijacking of an Air France jet in Algiers.
Air Algerie susequently cancelled its flights to Paris in a row with French officials over flight security, although it maintained service to the French cities of Lyon and Marseille.

The French authorities insisted on transfering Air Algerie's operations for security reasons to an isolated terminal at Charles de Gaulle airport to the north of Paris, from Orly airport to the city's south. Air Algerie refused, complaining that the new facilities discriminated against its passengers.

Officials said France had now agreed to move Air Algerie's flights to a regular terminal at Charles de Gaulle, and Algeria was eager to resume services in time for this year's summer flight schedule, which begins in April.
Only technical details involving office space, security arrangements and the allocation of take-off and landing slots remained to be resolved, they said.
French ties with Algiers worsened after a wave of bombings in France in 1995, blamed on Moslem fundamentalist rebels angry over French support for the army-backed Algerian authorities.
They were strained anew last month when French politicians called for greater deomcracy in Algeria, triggering an angry rejoinder from Algiers to keep out of its internal affairs.
